summary: Specifies the initial version of the iana-tunnel-type YANG module, which holds IANA-maintained identities used as interface types for tunnel interfaces. The module mirrors the IANA tunnelType registry, and new tunnel types are added by registering them with IANA.

eli5.summary: There is a list of tunnel kinds kept by an official registrar. This turns that list into a format network tools can read.

questions: what is the iana tunnel type yang module
how do i add a new tunnel type to yang
what yang identities exist for tunnels
subtitle: A YANG module that turns IANA's list of tunnel types into identities that network configuration models can reference.

tldr.problem: Network management models for tunnel interfaces need a standard, machine-readable way to say what kind of tunnel an interface is, and IANA already keeps a tunnelType registry that models could not use directly.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8675 defines the iana-tunnel-type YANG module, one identity per registry entry, each based on ift:tunnel. IANA keeps the module in step with the tunnelType registry.
tldr.outcome: Other YANG modules can refer to tunnel types such as gre, dslite or aplusp by identity. New types are added to the IANA registry, never directly to the module.

today: RFC 8675 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. The module's latest revision is maintained by IANA, which the RFC says can be obtained from the IANA website.

sections.title: Why a Tunnel Type Module
sections.content:
RFC 8675 specifies the initial version of the iana-tunnel-type YANG module. It holds a collection of IANA-maintained YANG identities that identify tunnel interface types. The module reflects IANA's tunnelType registry, which lives under the SMI Numbers registry, and the latest revision of the module can be obtained from the IANA website.

The RFC is deliberately narrow. Tunnel-specific extensions can be added to the Interface module (RFC 8343) depending on the tunnel type, but this document does not define such extensions for every encapsulation technology. Those are left to dedicated documents such as RFC 8676. It also does not try to bring the IANA registry up to a comprehensive list of tunnel technologies.

The module uses the common YANG types of RFC 6991 and follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA, RFC 8342).
sections.eli5: Many different kinds of tunnels exist. This RFC does not describe how each one works. It only gives each kind an official name that tools can use.

sections.title: The Module and Its Identities
sections.content:
The module imports iana-if-type from RFC 7224. Every tunnel type is a YANG identity whose base is ift:tunnel, so all of them count as tunnel interface types. Each identity carries a short description and a reference to the document that defines the tunnel.

The initial version covers tunnel types defined in RFC 4087, RFC 7856, RFC 7870 and RFC 6346. The identities are: other, direct, gre, minimal, l2tp, pptp, l2f, udp, atmp, msdp, sixtofour, sixoverfour, isatap, teredo, iphttps, softwiremesh, dslite and aplusp.

The module's first revision is dated 2019-11-16.
sections.eli5: Think of a sticker book with one sticker for each kind of tunnel: GRE, Teredo, DS-Lite and so on. A tool picks the right sticker for the tunnel it is working with.

sections.title: Keeping the Module and the Registry in Step
sections.content:
Tunnel type values must not be added directly to the YANG module. They must be added to the tunnelType subregistry, under the "ifType definitions" registry. When a type is added there, a new identity statement must be added to the module, and IANA has added notes to the registry and to the module saying so.

The identity name is the lower-case form of the matching enumeration in the IANAifType-MIB. Each identity has these sub-statements:

  • base contains ift:tunnel.
  • description replicates the description from the registry.
  • reference replicates the reference from the registry and adds the title of the document.

Unassigned or reserved values are not present in the module. Whenever the module is updated, a new revision statement must be added in front of the existing ones.

IANA also registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:iana-tunnel-type and the module name iana-tunnel-type with prefix iana-tunnel-type.
sections.eli5: The official list is the master copy. When a new kind of tunnel is added to the list, the registrar copies it into the machine-readable version, and nobody edits the copy by hand.

sections.title: Cleaning Up the tunnelType Registry
sections.content:
Section 4.2 shows IANA updating existing entries in the tunnelType registry. In the old table, the entries from 2 to 14 all cited RFC 4087, and entries 16 and 17 cited RFC 7856 and RFC 7870. In the new table, each type points at the RFC that actually defines the tunnel.

  • 2, direct: RFC 2003 and RFC 4213.
  • 3, gre: RFC 1701, RFC 1702 and RFC 7676.
  • 4, minimal: RFC 2004.
  • 5, l2tp: RFC 2661.
  • 6, pptp: RFC 2637.
  • 7, l2f: RFC 2341.
  • 8, udp: RFC 8085.
  • 11, sixToFour: RFC 3056.
  • 13, isatap: RFC 5214.

The remaining entries are updated in the same way, with one new reference each.
sections.eli5: The old list said "see this one book" for almost every tunnel. The new list points each tunnel at its own book.

sections.title: Example: Extending the Interface Module
sections.content:
Appendix A shows how the identities are used. An example module, example-iftunnel-extension, augments /if:interfaces/if:interface with a remote-endpoint leaf of type inet:ipv6-address. The augment applies only when the interface type is derived from iana-tunnel-type:gre, using the YANG when condition derived-from(if:type, 'iana-tunnel-type:gre').

This is the intended pattern: tunnel-specific settings are attached to a particular tunnel type by referring to its identity. It is an example only, not a module meant for implementation.
sections.eli5: If the sticker says "GRE tunnel", the tool also shows a box for "where does this tunnel end?". Other stickers would not show that box.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is designed to be accessed through network management protocols such as NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040). The mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH for NETCONF and TLS for RESTCONF, and the Network Configuration Access Control Model (RFC 8341) can restrict users to a subset of operations and content.

The module only defines identities meant to be referenced by other YANG modules. By themselves they expose no writable nodes, no read-only state and no RPCs, so the RFC concludes that there are no additional security issues to consider.
sections.eli5: This module is only a list of names. Nobody can change anything in the network by reading a list of names, so it adds no new risk.
